entry.title: How Domoticz Works: Inside the Open-Source Home Automation Server

link.title: How Domoticz Works: Inside the Open-Source Home Automation Server

entry.content:
Two hundred sensors report into one box. Zigbee door contacts, 433 MHz motion detectors, a MySensors temperature node on a battery, an HTTP weather poller — all of it converges on a single Domoticz process, and the dashboard keeps updating every few seconds. Then device #201 joins the mesh, scripts start firing late, and the usual “fix” is a nightly reboot and hope. If you have run a home automation server at any scale, you know exactly the afternoon this describes.

The reason Domoticz survives that kind of load is not magic, it is a specific and slightly unusual core design: every incoming sensor message crosses exactly two worker threads and one queue before it becomes a dashboard dot. Hardware adapters never touch the database. The database update is what triggers your Lua scripts — not the hardware, not the web layer. Once you see that separation, the whole repository reads like a well-rehearsed relay race.

We read the development branch line by line and traced one temperature reading from a serial gateway all the way to a fired script. Every claim below links into the real source on GitHub, and both diagrams were generated from the actual tree. If you want a comparable walkthrough of the interpreter that powers Domoticz’s plugin system, our CPython source tour covers that side.

Domoticz at a glance: one process, two worker threads, and everything speaking through queues, signals and one SQLite file.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process starts in main() at domoticz.cpp, L676, parses command line and config, installs SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers, and hands everything to m_mainworker.Start() at domoticz.cpp, L1241.
  • MainWorker::Start, L1136 fixes the startup order: database first (L1147), plugin system (L1158), hardware adapters (L1160), web servers (L1181).
  • Startup ends by spawning two threads: the main heartbeat loop (L1262) and a dedicated RX-message thread (L1264).
  • Every hardware adapter derives from CDomoticzHardwareBase, L13 and reports through one shared signal, sDecodeRXMessage at DomoticzHardware.h, L52.
  • The RX queue thread pops frames in Do_Work_On_Rx_Messages, L2016 and dispatches them into the giant protocol switch in ProcessRXMessage, L2098.
  • Decoded devices land in SQLite through CSQLHelper::UpdateValue, L5280, which delegates to UpdateValueInt, L5892.
  • The database update hands off to the event engine at SQLHelper.cpp, L5680, where ProcessDevice, L1644 queues work for Lua and dzVents scripts.
  • The web front-end binds its ports in CWebServer::StartServer, L153 and registers every /json.htm command via RegisterCommandCode, L354.
  • Python plugins are optional at build time; they are started only when ENABLE_PYTHON is compiled in (mainworker.cpp, L1158).

The detail view follows one message through the decoders, the SQL write, the event queue and back out through the web command table.

One hub, two worker threads, one RX queue

The design decision that keeps a 200-device hub responsive is deceptively small: hardware adapters are never allowed to process inline. When any adapter has a frame, it fires the sDecodeRXMessage signal — for example SendTempSensor, L179 packs a temperature struct and fires the signal with a byte buffer. MainWorker connected its own slot to that signal at startup (mainworker.cpp, L356), and the slot does almost nothing: DecodeRXMessage, L1891 pushes the raw bytes into a lock-free-ish concurrent_queue and returns. A chatty serial gateway can therefore produce messages as fast as the port delivers them without ever blocking on SQL.

The RX thread is where the real work happens. Do_Work_On_Rx_Messages, L2016 waits up to five seconds per pop, resolves the hardware object by id, then calls ProcessRXMessage (L2088). That function is a switch on the protocol byte at mainworker.cpp, L2110 — Lighting2, blinds, wind meters, security sensors, dozens of decoders, each one converting the raw buffer into device values. Only after a decoder succeeds does the worker announce the device by firing its own sOnDeviceReceived signal at mainworker.cpp, L2370 — which is exactly how the MQTT hardware, for instance, re-broadcasts updates (MQTT.cpp, L188). Inbound and outbound device changes share a funnel: the outbound path used by JSON commands, MainWorker::UpdateDevice, L14482, ultimately writes through the same SQL helper the RX thread uses.

There is one documented exception to the queue rule: shared “Domoticz-to-Domoticz” hardware with id 8765 decodes inline under a mutex (mainworker.cpp, L1895). Everything else queues.

Hardware: one base class, 149 adapters

Open the hardware/ folder and you find 149 .cpp files: RFXCOM serial and TCP, MySensors serial/MQTT/TCP, MQTT auto-discovery, Philips Hue, OpenZWave, an HTTP poller, and subfolders for 1-Wire, eHouse, openwebnet and others. All of them are small variations on one contract. CDomoticzHardwareBase gives each adapter a heartbeat thread (DomoticzHardware.cpp, L106), logging helpers, and about forty typed Send* methods that translate device semantics into the internal byte format. An adapter’s Start() spawns its own worker thread — see MySensorsSerial, L35 spawning its thread at L48 — and pushes bytes upward through the base-class signal.

Pull-style devices use the same contract in reverse. CHttpPoller has no serial line; its Do_Work, L76 loop fetches a URL on a timer and pushes the parsed values upward, so the rest of the system cannot tell whether a reading arrived by RF or by HTTP. The serial transport itself is a separate reusable layer: the AsyncSerial class at ASyncSerial.h, L26 with a setReadCallback hook that MySensors wires to its readCallback, L190, which parses node messages and calls SendSensor2Domoticz, L602 to emit typed sensors.

The plugin system sits on top of the same base class. CPluginSystem::StartPluginSystem, L82 boots an embedded CPython interpreter (the Py_Initialize call is at PluginManager.cpp, L153), and each Python plugin.py becomes a CPlugin — a hardware adapter — with its own message-pump thread (Plugins.cpp, L1225) draining command objects derived from CPluginMessageBase, L17. If you want to understand what Py_Initialize actually spins up, the CPython internals tour is the natural companion.

SQLite is the middle of the bus

Every decoded value, every timer tick, every JSON write ends in one place: CSQLHelper. The database opens first thing in startup (SQLHelper.cpp, L711) and owns the DeviceStatus table plus the shortlog tables that power the graphs. UpdateValue at SQLHelper.cpp, L5280 is the funnel: it resolves the device row by hardware/device-id/unit/type, inserts a fresh row on first sighting via InsertDevice, L5518, and finally delegates to UpdateValueInt, L5892, which updates DeviceStatus, refreshes logs and emits sOnDeviceReceived (the emit used by shared-user propagation is at SQLHelper.cpp, L11747).

The line that matters most for scripting is SQLHelper.cpp, L5680: only for devices marked as used, UpdateValueInt calls m_eventsystem.ProcessDevice(...). That single call means the event engine is downstream of the database, not of the hardware. A device that is not “used” never triggers scripts at all — a Domoticz gotcha that is obvious once you read this line and invisible otherwise. We traced the storage engine itself in the SQLite source tour if you want to know what happens underneath these calls.

The event engine: Lua, dzVents, and a 12-second heartbeat

CEventSystem::ProcessDevice at EventSystem.cpp, L1644 is the event gate. It first dedupes: for non-switch devices, an unchanged value only refreshes lastUpdate and returns (L1665) — a deliberate guard against faulty sensors that transmit ten times a second. Real changes get wrapped into _tEventQueue items and drained by the event thread started at StartEventSystem, L154. That worker (Do_Work, L350) does something unusual: it sleeps until the next multiple of twelve seconds (L381) so time-based scripts run on coarse, predictable boundaries, then handles minute-based logic on the minute.

Script execution has two layers. Classic Lua scripts run through EvaluateLuaClassic, L2894 inside a dedicated lua_State, with a watchdog thread (luaThread at L3377) so a looping script cannot hang the engine. Before any script runs, ExportDeviceStatesToLua, L2849 materialises all device states as Lua tables via the table builder at LuaTable.cpp, L23 — that is what makes domoticz.devices() work. dzVents is the friendlier layer on top, versioned in-code at dzVents.cpp, L47 (3.1.13) and routed through EvaluateDzVents, L56. There is no Python event path in this default flow — Python is reserved for the plugin system.

The same funnel serves the front door. The UI is a separate app under www/; what it talks to is a flat JSON command table. CWebServer::StartServer, L153 binds the HTTP and SSL ports (the accept loop lives in Do_Work at L102), and startup registers dozens of commands with RegisterCommandCode, L354 — each entry maps one /json.htm command name to a Cmd_* handler plus a minimum user-rights level. Cmd_GetVersion (WebServerCmds.cpp, L2695) is what the login screen probes first; the dashboard’s device list is Cmd_GetDevices, L4834. Control commands funnel into MainWorker::UpdateDevice, so a web click follows the same SQL and event path as an RF message — there is no ORM or request-object layer anywhere near what a Django app gives you, just functions that end in SQL.

From CMake 3.16 to a 15k-line worker: build facts

Measured on the development branch, the build is refreshingly explicit. The floor is CMake 3.16 (CMakeLists.txt, L2) with C++17 required (L64). Dependencies are pinned in text: Boost must be at least 1.69 (L16), Lua 5.3 is a hard requirement — the configure step literally tells you to apt-get install liblua5.3-dev if it is missing (L501) — and OpenSSL is REQUIRED (L673). SQLite can be either the system package or the bundled amalgamation behind the USE_BUILTIN_SQLITE option (L26), which refuses to configure without extern/sqlite-amalgamation present (L157). Plugin support needs the Python 3 development component (L512) and is otherwise compiled out.

The size distribution tells you where the project’s complexity actually lives: main/mainworker.cpp is 14,999 lines in this tree, main/SQLHelper.cpp is 12,623, and main/EventSystem.cpp is 4,775 — the hub, the storage funnel and the event engine are deliberately three huge files rather than many small ones. Versioning is date-based: appversion.h defines VERSION_MAJOR 2026, VERSION_MINOR 4 (appversion.h, L8), and this branch reports the beta channel (L17). The default branch here is development, not main — worth knowing before you cite line numbers.

Honest Limits

  • The plugin system is compile-time optional. Everything in the plugin section is guarded by #ifdef ENABLE_PYTHON (mainworker.cpp, L1158); a build without Python has no plugins at all.
  • One hardware type skips the queue: shared Domoticz hardware (id 8765) decodes inline under a mutex (mainworker.cpp, L1895), so the “everything queues” claim has this one carve-out.
  • Only used devices trigger events (SQLHelper.cpp, L5680); unused devices are stored but script-silent.
  • We traced dzVents only at its entry points (dzVents.cpp, L56); the user-facing dzVents framework files live in the top-level dzVents/ directory and were not covered here.
  • The www/ front-end application (its JS app, themes and templates) is out of scope; we covered only the JSON command layer it consumes.
  • Line numbers and file sizes were measured against the development branch head at publication time; this is an active branch and they will drift.
entry.summary: Trace one sensor message through Domoticz's open-source home automation server: RX queue, SQLite device store, Lua event engine, and the JSON API.

entry.title: How ESPHome Works: Inside the Compiler That Turns YAML into ESP32 Firmware

link.title: How ESPHome Works: Inside the Compiler That Turns YAML into ESP32 Firmware

entry.content:
You type esphome run device.yaml, wait about a minute, and the ESP32 on your desk is blinking. Two hundred lines of indentation-sensitive text went in; a megabyte of Xtensa machine code came out. Between those two moments there is no magic — there is a compiler: a Python program that validates your YAML against hundreds of schemas, translates every component into C++ objects, and hands the result to a real cross-toolchain.

The folklore says ESPHome “converts YAML into firmware” and stops there. That hides the interesting part: the intermediate representation. ESPHome does not paste your YAML into string templates. Each component’s to_code coroutine builds typed expression objects — variable declarations, calls, lambdas — that only get rendered to source text at the very end, so the tool knows which IDs point at which objects before a single line of C++ exists.

We read that compiler path in the repository’s own source to see exactly where your 200 lines go: the validation gauntlet, the code generation flow, the fixed setup()/loop() skeleton everything gets spliced into, and the protobuf-based native API the finished firmware speaks. Every claim below links to the file and line we verified.

ESPHome at a glance: YAML in, validated config, generated main.cpp, toolchain build, and a device runtime that serves the native API and accepts OTA updates.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Your YAML is parsed by yaml_util, which wraps secrets in a Sensitive type so keys never leak into logs or generated code.
  • read_config, L1778 is the entry point that loads and validates the file, returning None with a formatted error instead of a config.
  • validate_config, L1287 runs substitutions and packages first, then a priority-ordered queue of validation passes.
  • SchemaValidationStep, L986 checks every domain block against its CONFIG_SCHEMA via voluptuous schemas.
  • iter_component_configs, L62 yields each validated (domain, manifest, config) triple, expanding per-platform entries.
  • generate_cpp_contents, L812 schedules one to_code job per component and flushes the task queue.
  • Pvariable, L791 and add build the C++ expression tree that becomes your device objects.
  • write_cpp, L534 splices the rendered code into CPP_BASE_FORMAT, L39, the skeleton whose setup() calls App.setup().
  • compile_program, L849 dispatches to the ESP-IDF or PlatformIO backend; the flashed firmware runs Application::setup, L144.

The detail view: the validation passes, the expression-object code generator, the two toolchain backends, and the API/OTA stacks your binary ships with.

Validation: your YAML runs a gauntlet, not a schema check

validate_config is not one pass but a queue of ConfigValidationStep objects executed in priority order. Substitutions and packages are resolved first (config.py, steps 0 and 1 in the source), then auto-loads pull in dependencies each component declares, then the schema pass, then an ID pass, then cross-component final validation. A block like sensor: with a platform: dht entry is loaded, its platform manifest is resolved, and only then is the block handed to that platform’s schema.

The schema engine is voluptuous — All, L165 and Any subclass the library’s own combinators — but ESPHome layers real semantics on top: templatable() marks options that accept both literal values and runtime lambdas, update_interval() accepts 60s or 1min and returns a normalized time period, and validators like mac_address or ssid encode hardware rules in plain Python. If you have read our tour of CPython’s compiler internals, this will feel familiar: a parse tree refined pass by pass, except here the “ast” is your YAML dict with source ranges attached, which is why an invalid option reports the exact file and line you typed.

The ID pass deserves its own sentence: IDPassValidationStep, L1024 is where id: my_sensor references get bound. Automatic IDs are assigned when omitted, duplicates are rejected, and every cross-reference is checked to point at a declared object of the right type — before code generation, so a typo fails with a message, not a C++ compile error three layers deep.

The last pass is the only one that sees the whole device: FinalValidateValidationStep, L1215 runs each component’s cross-domain hook. This is where the OTA platform reconciles two ota: blocks that share a port, merges them, and refuses inconsistent encryption keys — checks that are impossible for any single schema, because they involve other domains’ config.

Code generation: every component becomes a C++ stanza

Code generation starts from the validated config, not your raw YAML. generate_cpp_contents, L812 walks iter_component_configs and adds one job per component that defines to_code. Each coroutine receives the validated dict for its domain and emits C++ through the cpp_generator expression classes: new_Pvariable declares an object, cg.add(var.set_port(...)) records a method call, process_lambda turns your YAML lambda into a real C++ lambda. These are objects with types and dependencies, not strings — that is how the generator knows a GPIOPin expression can be passed where a pin is expected.

One delightfully practical detail: _wrap_to_code, L772 wraps every to_code so the original YAML block lands in main.cpp as a comment right above the code it produced. The wrapper dumps the config with sort_keys=True — the comment explains that an unsorted dump would churn main.cpp and relink the firmware on every run even when nothing changed.

The accumulated statements land in CORE.cpp_main_section, and write_cpp_file, L829 hands them to the writer. Generation is not strictly sequential, either: each to_code is registered as a job on CORE via add_job, L1081 and flushed as a batch, so domains can emit in dependency order while ID references stay consistent. write_cpp reads the existing src/main.cpp, keeps whatever human-written sections live between the AUTO GENERATED markers, and splices in the new code — so you can edit the generated file’s outer regions and your edits survive the next esphome run. Lambdas get #line directives pointing back at your YAML, reset after each one by _reset_line_directives, L515, so a compiler error inside a lambda cites the YAML line you wrote.

From 200 lines of YAML to a 1 MB binary: build facts

The dev branch we read builds version 2026.12.0-dev (const.py, L7); the package targets Python 3.12–3.15. The core toolchain dependencies are pinned hard in requirements.txt: voluptuous 0.16.0, PyYAML 6.0.3, platformio 6.2.0, and esptool 5.6.0 for serial flashing. The component library is enormous — 866 directories under esphome/components/ — yet a minimal build compiles only the domains your YAML names, because generation is demand-driven from the validated config.

Compilation itself is dispatched per platform. ESP32/ESP-IDF builds go through espidf’s run_compile, L860, which drives idf.py and then produces factory and OTA images; Arduino/ESP8266 builds go through platformio’s run_compile, L369. A quirk worth knowing: writer.py has drifted from its name — today it is build-directory management (storage, cleaning, source-tree copying), and the actual main.cpp emission lives in __main__.py plus that one write_cpp function. Another: api_pb2.cpp, the protobuf codec, is committed to the repo but machine-generated — its header points at script/api_protobuf/api_protobuf.py, so editing wire messages by hand in the .proto alone is not enough.

The compile is also deliberately incremental: main.cpp is only recompiled when the configuration actually changed, as coroutine.py’s header, L15 spells out — generated code changes rarely, so the expensive C++ link is skipped on no-op runs. If you enjoy systems built as compiler plus codegen like this, our tour of Rust’s build architecture covers the other end of the trade: slower iteration, stronger runtime guarantees.

The runtime: App.setup() and the component contract

The firmware you flash has a tiny, boring entry point. The skeleton from CPP_BASE_FORMAT, L39 defines setup() that calls App.setup() and loop() that calls App.loop() — everything else is the framework. Application::setup walks every registered component in setup-priority order, calling its setup(), which is where a sensor reads its first value or Wi-Fi associates. Then App.loop() iterates the same component list forever; a Component is just virtual setup and loop, L154 plus an update interval and a status flag.

That contract is why the YAML vanishes at runtime. Nothing in the flashed binary parses configuration; every if your YAML expressed became a C++ conditional or a define compiled in (USE_OTA_ENCRYPTION, USE_API_HOMEASSISTANT_SERVICES, and friends are emitted during code generation). The cost is that behavior is fixed at build time; the benefit is a loop deterministic enough to run on 80 KB of RAM — and it is why two devices whose YAMLs differ compile to different binaries even from the same ESPHome version.

Talking to hubs: the native API and OTA

The api component is what makes the device a first-class citizen of Home Assistant. Its to_code, L584 registers the server, then emits defines for connection limits, batching delays, and the services you exposed. The wire format is protobuf over TCP, defined in api.proto, L111: a HelloRequest opens every connection, ListEntitiesRequest discovers what the device offers, and SubscribeStatesRequest, L558 streams state changes forever. The C++ codec in api_pb2.cpp is pre-generated, and each client gets an APIConnection object dispatching frames. If your hub is Domoticz rather than Home Assistant, there is no native API client yet — the practical bridge is MQTT, which we cover in our Domoticz setup tour.

OTA is a stack of two components. The shared ota base defines the component and its per-platform flash backends; the ota/esphome platform (to_code, L366) compiles in the protocol specifics: noise encryption keys shared with the API component, deflate for compressed uploads, and the response codes you can read in OTAResponseTypes, L18. The uploading side lives in the CLI at espota2.py, L33, with default ports per platform and the handshake state machine that probes a device before pushing an image.

Honest Limits

  • Everything here reads the dev branch at commit 904f0df (version 2026.12.0-dev). ESPHome moves fast; line numbers will drift, and some of these functions will be renamed by release.
  • We verified code, not hardware: no ESP32 was flashed for this post. The host platform can build and run the same generated program locally, but we did not execute it either.
  • The protobuf generation script (script/api_protobuf/) was not in our sparse checkout; the claim that api_pb2.cpp is generated comes from the generated file’s own header comment.
  • Toolchain acquisition (ESP-IDF downloads, PlatformIO packages) happens outside this repository, so version resolution of the actual compilers is not visible in the code we read.
  • The 866-component count and dependency pins are facts of the dev tree at read time; released versions differ.
entry.summary: Follow esphome run device.yaml through validation, C++ code generation, and the ESP32 toolchain build — read straight from the ESPHome compiler source.

entry.title: How Frigate NVR Works: Inside the Real-Time Camera AI Architecture

link.title: How Frigate NVR Works: Inside the Real-Time Camera AI Architecture

entry.content:
Every camera vendor wants a subscription. Nest, Ring, and their imitators all work the same way: pay monthly, or your “smart” camera stops being smart — and either way, every person detection runs on somebody else’s servers, so full-motion video of your driveway, hallway, and front door routinely leaves your network. Frigate inverts that deal. It is a self-hosted network video recorder that runs real-time object detection on hardware you already own — a CPU, a Coral Edge TPU, an Intel iGPU via OpenVINO, or an NVIDIA Jetson via TensorRT — and publishes events over MQTT that Home Assistant turns into automations. No account, no monthly fee, no third-party server.

This post is a guided tour of the actual source tree (the dev branch, commit 7fd81171f0b35bfe), with two diagrams generated directly from the repository. The overview diagram traces the ten moving parts that carry one frame from an RTSP stream to a Home Assistant event. The detail diagram goes a level deeper: the detector plugin contract, the shared-memory frame store, the watchdogs that keep it all alive, and the communicator layer that talks to your browser and your MQTT broker.

By the end you will know why Frigate runs cheap motion detection before expensive object detection, how a single accelerator serves every camera without duplicating GPU processes, where the fixed-size detection result arrays live, and what the MQTT contract between Frigate and Home Assistant looks like in code.

Frigate overview: capture → shared memory → per-camera analysis → detector processes → tracking → events → MQTT/API. Every node links to the exact source file on the dev branch.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • CameraCapture, L765 is one process per camera. It does not decode video in Python at all — ffmpeg handles RTSP, and Frigate reads raw YUV frames from ffmpeg’s stdout pipe.
  • capture_frames, L49 is the hot loop: readinto() fills a shared-memory slot directly (L88), then pushes (frame_name, timestamp) onto a queue with a non-blocking put (L111). If the queue is full, the frame is skipped (L112–115) rather than ever back-pressuring ffmpeg.
  • SharedMemoryFrameManager, L1063 is the reason those names mean anything: every frame lives in a named slot in /dev/shm, so capture, tracking, recording, and output all read the same bytes with zero copying.
  • CameraTracker, L116 is the per-camera analysis process, and process_frames, L242 is its main loop. This is where motion detection, region selection, inference requests, and object matching happen.
  • ImprovedMotionDetector, L15 runs first on every frame (detect.py L375). Frame differencing costs microseconds; running a neural network on the full frame would cost orders of magnitude more.
  • RemoteObjectDetector, L410 is the client half of inference: it copies a cropped region tensor into shared memory (L455), puts its slot name on the detection queue (L456), and blocks on a ZMQ notification that the result is ready (L457). Frames never travel through the queue — only a short name string.
  • ObjectDetectProcess, L327 owns one accelerator. Many cameras enqueue into it; it processes requests one at a time on the device it controls.
  • api_types, L29 is the plugin registry: every DetectionApi subclass is collected at import time and indexed by its config type string, so adding a detector is a matter of subclassing, not editing core code.
  • MqttClient, L39 publishes on a worker thread (publish, L83). When the broker is down, retained publishes are queued in memory (L88–92) and flushed on reconnect — Home Assistant never sees a missed state flip.

The detail view: detector plugins and their per-device runtime, the two watchdog layers, frame analysis internals, event and review processes, communicators, recording, and the web stack.

The Startup Order Is the Architecture

FrigateApp.start() reads like a table of contents for the whole system, and the order is deliberate. Detectors come first: start_detectors, L393 pre-creates the per-camera input and output shared-memory blocks (a fixed 20×6 float32 result buffer per camera, L405–407), then builds one ObjectDetectProcess per configured accelerator (L426), each configured by build_detector_config, L61, which parses a device string — a /dev/apex_0 path, a PCI slot, a /dev/dri/renderD128 render node — into a concrete plugin config.

Then the service layer boots: the dispatcher (L686), video output (L696), the tracked-object processor (L698), and finally start_camera_processor, L461, which hands each camera to CameraMaintainer, L29. The maintainer starts a capture process (its __start_camera_capture at L154 pre-creates ten frame slots per camera at L164–167) and a tracker process per camera. Only after all of that does create_fastapi_app, L69 get served by uvicorn on 127.0.0.1:5001 (L718, L735–736) behind nginx.

Two watchdog layers keep this alive. FrigateWatchdog, L42 restarts any registered process through its factory (L101–102), and separately checks whether a detector has been stuck mid-inference for over ten seconds — if so it calls start_or_restart() (L122–126). Inside each capture process, CameraWatchdog, L141 watches frame staleness and restarts ffmpeg when a stream stalls.

Why Motion Detection Runs Before Object Detection

The core cost asymmetry of video AI is this: frame differencing is nearly free, neural inference is not. Frigate exploits it ruthlessly. In process_frames, the very first thing that happens to a decoded frame is motion_detector.detect(frame) — ImprovedMotionDetector, L15 computes motion boxes with pixel-level differencing, supporting masks and a calibration period on startup.

Those motion boxes, merged with the boxes of already-tracked objects, become detection regions: get_cluster_region consolidates candidates into a handful of rectangles sized against the model’s minimum region (L423–430). Standalone motion outside existing regions gets its own grid-informed regions (L443–465), and a startup scan sweeps the full frame once (L467–473). Only then does Frigate run detect() per region (L490–501): crop, resize to model input, infer, and map boxes back to full-frame coordinates (L221–224), then merge overlapping detections with reduce_detections (L503) and hand everything to the tracker via match_and_update (L511). This is why an idle Frigate with live cameras sits at near-zero CPU: full inference runs only when something moved.

One Detector Process, Many Cameras

The most economical trick in the codebase is detector sharing. app.py L111 creates one mp.Queue per model “scene”; every camera configured with that model drops its requests into the same queue. Each accelerator runs exactly one DetectorRunner, L133: its run loop (L159) pulls a connection id, map_input_frame, L116 turns that name into the tensor, detect_raw runs the plugin (L188), and the fixed-size result block — up to 20 detections, each 6 floats — is written straight into the requesting camera’s output shared memory (L194) before a ZMQ ping wakes the waiting camera (L195).

No frame data is ever pickled through a multiprocessing queue; the queue carries a camera-name string, and the heavy bytes move through shared memory. For accelerators that queue requests internally, there is an asynchronous variant, AsyncDetectorRunner, L204, which splits submission and result collection into separate worker threads (_detect_worker at L234). The tracker side keeps identity across frames with NorfairTracker, L115, combining centroid motion with histogram appearance (frigate_distance, L86). If you want to understand why these multiprocessing queues and shared-memory blocks behave the way they do under the hood, we’ve covered the foundations in our CPython internals deep dive.

From Docker Image to Detector Plugin

The build system mirrors the runtime plugin split. The docker/ directory is effectively a matrix of accelerator images: the base docker/main/Dockerfile plus build_ov_model.py and requirements-ov.txt for Intel OpenVINO targets; docker/tensorrt/Dockerfile.amd64 and Dockerfile.arm64 for Jetson; dedicated images for Rockchip (RKNN), ROCm, Raspberry Pi, and Synaptics; and user_installation.sh scripts for Hailo, Memryx, and DeepX boards. At runtime the choice is pure data — api_types collects all DetectionApi subclasses at import time (detector_types.py, L29), so the plugin file just needs to exist and subclass.

The current tree ships 14 plugin files. The ones most people run: CpuTfl, L41 on tflite-runtime for CPU-only boxes; EdgeTpuTfl, L40 for the Coral USB/PCIe TPU; OvDetector, L37 with dedicated YOLO post-processing (process_yolo at L142) for Intel iGPUs; and TensorRtDetector, L85, which allocates explicit GPU host/device buffers and runs _do_inference (L194) for NVIDIA. The web UI is a separate Vite + React app (web/src/App.tsx, with Live, Events, Explore, and Settings pages) that talks to the FastAPI backend and to WebSocket streams from api/ws.ts; live video itself is proxied by go2rtc, installed into the image by docker/main/install_go2rtc.sh.

Events, Review Segments, and the Home Assistant Contract

Once tracking produces a stable object, the event machinery takes over. Each camera’s tracker feeds detected_frames_queue into TrackedObjectProcessor, L58 — the central thread that decides which frames become snapshots (should_save_snapshot at L270), which become MQTT snapshot payloads (L317), and which become manually created events (L570). EventProcessor, L69 persists event start/end rows into SQLite — and on boot closes any event left open by a crash (L87–89). In parallel, ReviewProcess, L14 builds review segments that power the UI timeline, and RecordProcess, L17 writes recording segments for playback and export.

Everything user-visible leaves through Dispatcher, L63, the switchboard between Frigate internals and its communicators. Its publish (L490) fans object updates, stats, and review segments out to MqttClient and WebSocketClient, L582; inbound MQTT commands for the ~20 camera settings it registers (L93–115) flow back the other way, including live config changes like toggling detection or editing masks without restarts. The MQTT contract Home Assistant relies on is simple: every topic is prefixed (mqtt.py L85), availability and camera states are published retained, and if the broker drops, retained messages are queued and replayed on reconnect. That retained-topic pattern is exactly what makes zero-config discovery work in Home Assistant — and it is the same pattern you can reuse to wire Frigate events into Node-RED flows for automations, or into Domoticz event scripts if that is your hub of choice.

Honest Limits

  • Single host by design. The zero-copy frame store lives in /dev/shm; the capture, analysis, and detection processes must share one machine. There is no distributed mode in this codebase.
  • The API is not meant to be exposed. uvicorn binds 127.0.0.1:5001 (app.py L735–736) and expects nginx in front for TLS and auth. Pointing a browser at the Python port directly bypasses that design.
  • CPU detection is the floor, not the target. CpuTfl works, but the entire motion-first region design exists because full-frame neural inference at camera frame rates is only realistic on dedicated silicon.
  • Result buffers are fixed-size. Each detection request returns at most 20 rows of 6 floats (app.py L405–407); dense scenes rely on region consolidation and thresholding rather than unlimited outputs.
  • Restart storms are capped. The watchdog gives a process 5 restarts per 60 seconds (watchdog.py L16–17) before backing off — a genuinely flaky accelerator will go quiet instead of thrashing forever.
  • Expect a warm-up. The motion detector calibrates on startup before trusting its own boxes, so detection quality in the first minutes after a restart is not representative.
entry.summary: How Frigate NVR runs local object detection: ffmpeg capture, shared-memory frames, CPU/Coral/OpenVINO/TensorRT detectors, MQTT events and Home Assistant.

entry.title: How Homebridge Works: Inside the HomeKit Bridge Architecture

link.title: How Homebridge Works: Inside the HomeKit Bridge Architecture

entry.content:
You spend a weekend wiring a garage door relay, a cheap Zigbee bulb set, and an off-brand robot vacuum into something controllable — then open the Apple Home app and find none of them. HomeKit is a walled garden by design: it only talks to accessories that speak the HomeKit Accessory Protocol (HAP) and, in practice, carry Apple’s MFi certification. Thousands of excellent devices will never be in that club. Homebridge is the open-source project that quietly ended the argument years ago: a Node.js server that impersonates a genuine HomeKit bridge, so uncertified devices of every kind appear in the Home app as if Apple had blessed them. Pair it with Zigbee2MQTT and the radio side of the house stays open too.

This post dissects how that impersonation works, using two architecture diagrams generated from the homebridge/homebridge repository (default branch latest, version 2.5.0). The overview shows the moving parts; the detail diagram traces the startup chain down to individual functions in src/server.ts, src/pluginManager.ts, src/bridgeService.ts, and src/childBridgeFork.ts, every node linking to real source.

By the end you will know exactly why the boot order is cache → plugins → platforms → publish, why a plugin’s registerAccessory() call only works during initialization, how cached accessory UUIDs survive restarts, what a _bridge config block spawns, and where the new Matter support fits.

Overview: one Server orchestrating plugins, a single HAP Bridge accessory, the accessory cache, and forked child bridges. Every node links to real source in homebridge/homebridge@latest.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process entry point is cli(), L28: it parses flags, points HAPStorage at the persist directory at L73, and only then constructs the Server at L87.
  • Server.start, L208 runs a fixed boot sequence — cache, plugins, platforms, child bridges, and only then the publication that makes it visible to HomeKit.
  • HomebridgeAPI, L635 is one EventEmitter (API version 2.7) handed to every plugin; the registerAccessory overload at L814 converts plugin calls into internal events rather than direct wiring.
  • new Bridge, L334 creates the thing HomeKit actually pairs with: a single hap-nodejs Bridge accessory named from config.json, with the fixed UUID uuid.generate('HomeBridge').
  • publishBridge, L374 builds a PublishInfo (username, port, pincode, Categories.BRIDGE) and calls bridge.publish() at L406.
  • loadCachedPlatformAccessoriesFromDisk, L417 and restoreCachedPlatformAccessories, L483 are the cache halves: read serialized accessories before plugins load, then replay each one into configureAccessory().
  • ChildBridgeService, L216 supervises one forked Node process per _bridge config, created with a real fork() at L424.
  • The protocol itself lives in the @homebridge/hap-nodejs, L53 dependency; this repo is the plugin host and config layer around it.

Detail: the startup chain from cli() through plugin initialization and cache restore to HAP publication, plus the child-bridge fork path. Node labels link to exact lines in the repository.

The Bridge Trick: One HomeKit Accessory for Everything

HAP defines a special accessory type — a bridge — that proxies many bridged accessories over one pairing. Homebridge exploits that to the hilt: you pair once, with the QR code printed by printSetupInfo, L1265, and everything every plugin exposes rides behind that single pairing. The defaults come from loadConfig, L362: bridge name Homebridge, username CC:22:3D:E3:CE:30, PIN 031-45-154 (L366–L370). The username must look like a MAC address — the check at L424 rejects anything else, because hap-nodejs uses it as the pairing identity.

For legacy accessory plugins, each configured instance becomes a hap-nodejs accessory via createHAPAccessory, L768. It calls the plugin’s getServices() at L769, and if the plugin returns an empty set the accessory is silently dropped at L774 — a common source of “my accessory vanished” bug reports. The stable UUID is derived from the accessory type and name at L780, which is why renaming an accessory in config makes HomeKit treat it as a new device.

The Startup Chain: Command to Published Bridge

The detail diagram’s left half is worth internalizing: almost every startup bug is a violation of it. cli() constructs the Server, whose constructor parses the config, creates exactly one HomebridgeAPI, L119 per process, then a PluginManager, L139 and a BridgeService, L151. start() then runs in a fixed order at L208:

  1. Cache first: loadCachedPlatformAccessoriesFromDisk, L216 — so serialized accessories exist in memory before any plugin runs.
  2. Plugins second: initializeInstalledPlugins, L238 imports each plugin and runs its default-exported initializer.
  3. Platforms and accessories third: loadPlatforms, L571 and loadAccessories at L265–L270, with dynamic platforms registered but not yet replayed.
  4. Child bridges start at L273, then cache replay via restoreCachedPlatformAccessories at L278.
  5. api.signalFinished() at L281 emits didFinishLaunching — the event plugins wait for before polling hardware — followed by await Promise.all(promises) at L284 so legacy static platforms finish before publishBridge, L286.

That last ordering is a compatibility contract with the oldest plugin style: a StaticPlatformPlugin hands over accessories through a callback, and loadPlatformAccessories, L817 waits for it while warning every 20 seconds at L821 if a plugin is stalling the whole bridge.

The Plugin API: Three Flavours, One Funnel

Every plugin is an npm package whose default export is a function receiving the api object. initializeInstalledPlugins, L199 iterates discovered plugins, calls plugin.load() (which validates the engines.homebridge requirement and dynamically imports the entry point at L220), then initializePlugin, L235 invokes the initializer with the API instance at L238.

One guard rail worth knowing: handleRegisterAccessory, L255 throws if a plugin registers outside a running initializer — “register later, on a timer” plugins crash.

Homebridge classifies platform plugins by duck-typing, not by declared interface. isDynamicPlatformPlugin, L798 checks whether configureAccessory exists on the instance; isStaticPlatformPlugin, L802 checks for the legacy accessories callback. loadPlatforms, L658 branches on that: dynamic platforms get stored via assignDynamicPlatform, static ones join the awaited promise list, and independent platforms (like config UIs) just get constructed.

Dynamic platforms then manage their own accessories through the API: registerPlatformAccessories, L855 stamps each accessory with _associatedPlugin and _associatedPlatform at L862 before emitting the internal event that BridgeService subscribed to in its constructor at L329. The same pattern handles updates, unregistration, and external accessories — IP cameras and TVs that get their own HAPServer outside the bridge.

The Accessory Cache: Why UUIDs Survive Restarts

HomeKit hates churn: change an accessory’s UUID and the user re-configures rooms, automations, and notifications. Homebridge’s answer is a disk cache at ~/.homebridge/accessories/cachedAccessories, resolved by User.cachedAccessoryPath, L23 over the ~/.homebridge base at L32.

The read path is defensive. loadCachedPlatformAccessoriesFromDisk, L417 reads through the StorageService at L421; on a JSON SyntaxError it falls back to the .cachedAccessories.bak backup named at L452, which is written after every successful load at L441. Each record becomes a PlatformAccessory, L37 — an EventEmitter mirroring a hap-nodejs accessory, with a plugin-writable context field at L55 that survives serialization.

The restore path restoreCachedPlatformAccessories, L483 replays each cached accessory into the matching dynamic platform’s configureAccessory(), and even survives plugin renames: if the recorded _associatedPlugin is missing, L511 searches for a plugin with an active dynamic platform of the same name and rewrites the association. Writes happen at every mutation — L600 for register, L674 for update, L690 for unregister — and once more during teardown at L859, right before the shutdown event reaches plugins.

Child Bridges: One Process Per Plugin

A single misbehaving plugin can block the event loop of the entire bridge, since the process shares one Node.js runtime (see how Node.js works). The escape hatch is the _bridge block in config.json. When loadAccessories, L507 or loadPlatforms, L617 sees _bridge.username, the plugin is routed into a ChildBridgeService, L525 instead of the main bridge, tracked in a map keyed by MAC-style username at L84.

validateChildBridgeConfig, L674 enforces uniqueness: a child username must be valid, must not collide with the main bridge, and each platform child bridge needs its own identity. At runtime the service forks childBridgeFork.js at L424; inside that child, loadPlugin, L88 strips _bridge keys from the config, builds a fresh HomebridgeAPI, L122, and loads exactly one plugin. The child then assembles its own BridgeService at L201 and publishes an independent HomeKit bridge with its own port and pairing code. Restart, stop, and start commands arrive over IPC (L801, L815, L836) — that is how homebridge-config-ui-x restarts one plugin without touching the parent.

From HAP-Only Monolith to Matter-Era Architecture

The build facts tell the story of a decade-long shift. Homebridge began as a monolith containing the entire HAP implementation; today package.json declares version 2.5.0 with @homebridge/hap-nodejs 2.3.0 as a dependency at L53, and the old lib/ HAP sources are gone — under src/types/ only a qrcode-terminal type stub remains. The plugin-facing API has incremented to version 2.7 (L636), and engines now requires Node.js ^22.12.0 || ^24 || ^26 at L33 — the codebase has fully moved to ES modules with dynamic import() for plugin loading.

The bigger leap is Matter. Homebridge 2.x ships an opt-in Matter bridge: Server.start() only dynamically imports MatterBridgeManager, L246 when a bridge.matter block exists, deliberately avoiding the heavy @matter/main stack for HAP-only installs. Plugins get a parallel API surface — the api.matter getter at L689 returns undefined unless Matter is configured, and dynamic platforms can implement configureMatterAccessory at L129 alongside their HAP counterpart. Matter accessories keep their own MatterAccessoryCache, L74, mirroring the HAP cache design. Matter control requests even route to child bridges over IPC, reusing the fork infrastructure built for HAP isolation.

If you want to go further than switching lights, the same pattern composes: Homebridge for HomeKit translation, Node-RED for event-driven automations across both HomeKit and non-HomeKit devices.

Honest Limits

  • No HAP code lives here. Everything protocol-level — pairing, encryption, characteristic I/O, mDNS — is the @homebridge/hap-nodejs dependency. This repo is config validation, plugin lifecycle, and cache management only.
  • Static plugins can stall the boot. A legacy platform that never calls the accessories callback blocks publication; Homebridge only warns every 20 seconds (L821) rather than timing it out.
  • Empty plugin responses vanish silently. An accessory plugin whose getServices() returns nothing is skipped without an error at L774 — by design, but confusing the first time.
  • Orphaned cache entries need -K. Cached accessories whose plugin no longer loads are dropped unless keepOrphanedCachedAccessories is set (cli.ts L50).
  • The default is one shared process. Without _bridge blocks, all plugins run on the main event loop; a blocking plugin delays didFinishLaunching for everything else.
  • Matter is opt-in and partial. Accessory-style child bridges do not support Matter at all — startBridge() warns and ignores the config at L158–L160.

Homebridge’s lesson for anyone building protocol adapters: keep the protocol engine in a dedicated library, expose a narrow event-based API to plugins, and make identity (UUIDs, cache, pairing) explicit and durable. That structure is why thousands of community plugins have outpaced any vendor’s official integration list.
entry.summary: How Homebridge emulates a HomeKit bridge in Node.js: HAP pairing, the plugin API, accessory caching, child bridges and Matter support, traced from the source.

entry.title: How Node-RED Works: Inside the Flow Engine and Runtime Architecture

link.title: How Node-RED Works: Inside the Flow Engine and Runtime Architecture

entry.content:
Every smart home starts the same way: a Python script polling one vendor API, a cron job pushing to another, a MQTT subscriber copied from a blog post, and a folder of half-finished glue scripts nobody dares to delete. Each integration works alone, none of them share state, and when one throws an exception at 3 a.m. the others keep running blind. Node-RED’s core idea was to make the wiring itself the artifact — drag nodes onto a canvas, connect them into a flow, press Deploy — but the reason it survived a decade of alternatives is the runtime underneath: a tiny, disciplined engine that routes messages between nodes with predictable semantics, persists flows to disk, and restarts exactly the pieces you changed.

This post walks that engine in the real source (node-red/node-red, branch main, HEAD e4f7fc516cd8, checked 2026-11-15) with two generated call graphs. The overview shows the moving parts: the CLI bootstrap, the editor API and its WebSocket channel, the runtime API layer, the flow engine, the node registry, and the context stores. The detail view goes one level deeper — the deploy cycle from POST /flows to running flows, and the full journey of one message from node.send() to the next node’s input callback.

By the end you will know where a Deploy button click actually lands in code, why a fan-out to five branches clones the message but a linear chain does not, how context.get("myvar") finds its store, and why the runtime mounts two separate express apps on two separate URL roots. The story is a good companion to our earlier Domoticz tour — two very different answers to the same home-automation problem.

Overview: the CLI boots lib/red.js, which wires the runtime and the editor API into one express server; the editor talks to the runtime through an admin REST API plus a WebSocket bus; the flow manager instantiates Flow objects that route messages between Node instances resolved from the registry.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap is two packages wired together by hand. init, L57 receives the HTTP server from the CLI, then calls runtime.init, L73 and api.init, L75 in sequence and merges the two express apps with api.httpAdmin.use(runtime.httpAdmin), L77. There is no service locator — just three requires at L20–23 and a handful of function calls.
  • The runtime start chain is an explicit promise chain of subsystems. start, L135 registers the i18n catalog, then initializes storage, settings, telemetry, library and multiplayer (L136–141), loads node types with redNodes.load(), L166 and only then loads and starts the flows (L241–244). Order matters: no node types exist before the registry loads, and no flows run before contexts are ready.
  • One process, two express apps, two URL roots. nodeApp and adminApp are created at L94–95; the CLI mounts adminApp at httpAdminRoot (L423) and nodeApp at httpNodeRoot (L435). That separation is why your HTTP-in endpoints can sit behind different auth and a different path prefix than the editor.
  • send is optimized by wiring shape. updateWires, L89 inspects the wires array: an unwired node gets its send replaced by NOOP_SEND, L101, and a node with exactly one output and one target gets a cached _wire, L107 so the hot path skips all iteration.
  • One message hop is a SendEvent flowing through hook stages. Node.send, L381 builds an array of send events — one per output-per-wire — and hands them to this._flow.send, L491; Flow.send, L715 runs onSend → preRoute → preDeliver hooks (handleOnSend, L790). Cloning is precise: the clone flag is set only from the second send onward (L466), and preRoute clones per branch when needed (L813–815).
  • Delivery is deferred by exactly one tick. handlePreDeliver, L831 wraps delivery in setImmediate, L839 unless runtimeSyncDelivery forces synchronous mode (L858). Deep chains therefore never recurse through the stack — each hop is a fresh macrotask.
  • The editor talks REST plus WebSocket, not one or the other. Flow CRUD rides the admin API (GET/POST /flows, L43–44); live traffic — status updates, notifications, debug messages — rides a WebSocket server attached via server.on('upgrade'), L237 at <adminRoot>/comms, with per-connection sends batched on a 50 ms timer (_queueSend, L192).
  • The runtime mirrors internal events back to every editor. publish, L77 fans node-status and runtime-event emissions out to all connections, keeping a retained map that replays on subscribe (L153–163). This is why a second browser tab sees the same node status dots as the first.
  • Node types are a registry, filled by a disk scanner. load, L36 asks the local-filesystem module for node sets in core dirs and the userDir node_modules tree; registerNodeConstructor, L435 rejects duplicate type names and emits type-registered (L461) — the event that unblocks flows sitting on missing types.

Detail view: the deploy path (editor → admin routes → mutex-guarded flows API → diff, save, stop, start) on the left, and the message path (Node.send → flow hook stages → setImmediate → receive → input callback → done) on the right, with the registry and context stores underneath.

The deploy cycle: from editor click to running flows

When you press Deploy, the editor sends POST /flows with a Node-RED-Deployment-Type header — full, nodes, flows, or reload (L50). The runtime API layer serializes everything behind an async-mutex, L37 so two concurrent deploys cannot interleave (setFlows, L66–67). Optimistic concurrency is built in: if the editor’s rev does not match the active revision, the deploy fails with version_mismatch and HTTP 409 (L78–84) — that is the “another user has modified your flows” dialog reduced to five lines.

The real work happens in setFlows, L118: the config is cloned, parsed, and compared against the active config via diffConfigs, L154, which classifies every node as added, changed, removed, rewired, or linked. Credentials are exported and the whole config is written through storage.saveFlows, L202 before anything is restarted. Only then does the manager stop, L220 the affected flows, clean up orphaned context (L222), and start, L228 the new config.

The deploy type determines the blast radius. A full deploy creates a Flow object for the global config (L357) plus one per tab (L365); a modified-nodes or modified-flows deploy calls update on the flows that changed, L385–390 and leaves untouched tabs running. Each surviving await activeFlows[id].start(diff), L402 then rebuilds only what the diff says: new nodes are instantiated, rewired nodes just get updateWires applied, and closed nodes run their close callbacks under a 15-second timeout (stopNode, L768–778).

Inside one message hop: node.send to the next input

Follow one message through the detail diagram. (1) The sending node’s send, L381 stamps a fresh _msgid on first send (L397–399), takes the single-wire shortcut when possible (L393–414), and otherwise walks every output and wire building SendEvents (L429–475). (2) Flow.send runs the hook stages: onSend once for the batch (L792), preRoute per event, which resolves the destination via flow.getNode, L811 and clones the message for fan-out branches. (3) preDeliver schedules the hand-off inside setImmediate, L838–841. (4) deliverMessageToDestination, L821 calls destination.node.receive(msg). (5) receive, L499 stamps _msgid if missing and emits input, which routes into _emitInput, L201: the onReceive hook fires first (L206), then your node’s callback runs as input(msg, send, done) (L214–218).

The done callback is the modern completion contract. Calling done() routes through _complete, L132, which triggers the onComplete hook and asks the flow to notify any complete nodes wired downstream (handleComplete, L698); calling done(err) instead goes to handleError, L596, which dispatches to catch nodes. Errors thrown synchronously inside the input callback are caught and logged rather than crashing the process (L219–221). Because every hop lands in a fresh macrotask, this design composes cleanly with the event loop — if you want the underlying model, our Node.js event loop walkthrough covers the mechanics this engine leans on. Node-RED adds one hard backstop on top: an uncaught exception anywhere still terminates the whole process (red.js, L525–541).

Context: where flow state actually lives

Node-RED gives every node three context scopes — node-local, flow, and global — and the implementation is lazier than you might expect. Node.prototype.context(), L119 creates the node’s context object on first use, keyed by nodeId:flowId (getContext, L520), and attaches flow and global as read-only properties (L540–546). Flow-level contexts are created in the Flow constructor itself (L64), with $parent traversal for subflow nesting.

Which store backs those lookups is a settings decision. load, L69 reads settings.contextStorage, instantiates each configured plugin, and lets a key name pick a store inline — context.get("cache","myredis") style, where parseContextStore splits the store from the key (L299–302). The default is the Memory store, L19: a plain object per scope, fast and intentionally non-persistent. Everything else — file-backed, or third-party stores such as a Redis connector for cross-restart shared state — plugs into the same two-method interface. During a deploy, orphaned contexts are pruned by clean, L591 against the known node set, and the admin API exposes /context/:scope/:id read routes (L79–82) so you can inspect live state without adding a debug node.

From single-file demo to a v5 monorepo

The repository shape tells the maturity story. Since the 1.x restructure, the code is a pnpm-style monorepo under packages/node_modules/: @node-red/runtime, @node-red/editor-api, @node-red/registry, @node-red/util, @node-red/nodes (the core node set — inject, debug, function, catch, template and friends), @node-red/editor-client (the browser editor source), and a thin node-red CLI wrapper on top. The root package.json names the whole thing node-red at version 5.0.9, L2–3, marked private because the packages are published individually, and hard-pins the runtime: "node": ">=22.9", L134. The CLI enforces the same floor twice — once with semver.satisfies, L30 and again inside lib/red.js — and refuses to start otherwise.

First-run ergonomics are equally concrete. With no settings file found, the CLI copies its bundled default settings.js into ~/.node-red — but only if the default has not been modified on disk, checked by comparing mtime against ctime (L149–156) — so upgrades never silently overwrite your config. The same binary doubles as an admin client: node-red admin ... short-circuits into the node-red-admin package (L18–27). And for embedded use, running with both HTTP roots disabled logs server.headless-mode and skips server.listen entirely (L513–515) — the engine still runs flows, just with no network surface. Test hygiene matches the split: unit tests are separated into mocha:core and mocha:nodes suites (package.json, L20–22), and linting covers only the editor client sources (L17).

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers drift. Everything above was verified against main at HEAD e4f7fc516cd8 (2026-11-15); the architecture is durable, the line anchors are not.
  • The core node set here is small on purpose. The repo ships @node-red/nodes/core (common, function, sequence, parser, network, storage groups), but the hundreds of palette nodes — MQTT brokers, GPIO, dashboard widgets — are separate npm modules resolved from userDir/node_modules at load time (loader.js, L36–44). Reading this repo will not show you how your specific third-party node behaves.
  • One process, one point of failure. All flows run in a single Node process; the uncaughtException handler logs and calls process.exit(1) (red.js, L525–541). There is no per-flow isolation, no worker threads, no failover in this codebase.
  • The default context store is volatile. Unless you configure contextStorage, all context lives in a plain JavaScript object and vanishes on restart (memory.js, L19–21). Persistence is a configuration step, not a default.
  • This post skips subflow internals. Subflow.js instances wrap the same Node machinery with aliasing (_alias in Node.js, L50–52), but instance creation and env inheritance in Subflow.js deserve their own tour.
entry.summary: Node-RED internals from source: the runtime core, node registry, message passing between nodes, context stores, admin API vs HTTP nodes, and the deploy cycle.

entry.title: How openHAB Works: Inside the OSGi Smart Home Core Architecture

link.title: How openHAB Works: Inside the OSGi Smart Home Core Architecture

entry.content:
Ask anyone who has owned two smart home hubs why they replaced the first one, and the answer is rarely the hardware: it is the model. Every hub invents its own vocabulary for “a lamp,” ships its own rules language, and refuses to talk to the neighbors’ protocols — so your Z-Wave stick, your Hue bridge and your MQTT sensors each need a separate integration with a separate device model, and when a vendor sunsets a hub the whole abstraction dies with it. openHAB’s bet, refined over fifteen years, is that this problem is structural: put one device model and one event bus inside a Java process, and make every driver a replaceable module around them.

That bet is visible in the repository this post walks: openhab/openhab-core, branch main at HEAD 15c6da97b24e (checked 2026-11-15), roughly 100 OSGi bundle modules and 2,550 Java files of pure framework — no device drivers, no UI chrome. Two generated architecture graphs accompany the text: an overview of the moving parts, then a detail view of the wiring that carries one command from a UI toggle to a device handler and one state change back.

By the end you will know where a button press becomes an event, how an item command finds the right handler through a profile indirection, how the rule engine runs composable trigger/condition/action graphs, why discovered devices land in an inbox before they become Things, and what the OSGi module system buys that a plain monolithic framework would not.

Overview: the org.openhab.core base bundle declares the Item and Event contracts; the thing bundle models devices plus their handlers; CommunicationManager routes item commands and updates through per-link profiles; everything crosses one OSGi EventAdmin event bus; the rule engine and discovery hang off the same bus.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The device model is three small interfaces, not a class hierarchy. Thing, L42 is documented as “a representation of a connected part (e.g. physical device or cloud service)” and amounts to channels, configuration, status and properties (getChannels(), L82). Channel, L42 carries the item type it accepts plus a kind (getKind(), L107) that separates state channels from trigger channels, and Bridge extends Thing, L28 lets a hub host child Things.
  • Nothing calls a device driver directly — everything rides one event bus. OSGiEventPublisher, L38 implements the openHAB EventPublisher, L24 contract by wrapping the standard OSGi EventAdmin and posting every event on a single "openhab" topic (eventAdmin.postEvent(...), L69). On the receive side, OSGiEventManager, L44 declares "event.topics:String=openhab", deserializes payloads through registered factories, and fans out to each EventSubscriber.receive(), L58 that subscribed to the event type.
  • Items and Things are decoupled on purpose. Item, L38 never mentions devices: it is state plus accepted command types (getState(), L45). The join point is ItemChannelLink, L29 — an item name plus getLinkedUID(), L57 — and CommunicationManager, L97 implements both EventSubscriber and the link-registry change listener, keeping a per-link profile cache warm (L204).
  • Commands cross exactly one transform layer: profiles. A configured link can pin a profile (getConfiguredProfileTypeUID, L228); otherwise advisors and the system default factory decide (L246). The default profile ends the trip at onCommandFromItem, L377, which lands in the handler’s handleCommand(ChannelUID, Command), L101 — the one method every binding must implement.
  • The framework, not the binding, owns the lifecycle. ThingRegistryImpl, L55 notifies all ThingTrackers on every add or update (L213); ThingManagerImpl, L124 picks the factory whose supportsThingType(), L40 matches, calls registerHandler(Thing), L55, and runs doInitializeHandler(), L737 under SafeCaller timeout guards — a hung binding degrades one Thing, not the process.
  • States come back as events, with a policy for self-echo. A handler’s updateState(), L324 becomes an ItemStateEvent on the topic template openhab/items/{itemName}/state (L54), while commands on openhab/items/{itemName}/command (L52) pass through AutoUpdateManager.receiveCommand(), L138, which can echo the command as state when the channel declares an auto-update policy.
  • Rules are data: composable modules that subscribe like everyone else. A Rule, L47 is a graph of Trigger, L41, Condition, L43 and Action, L42 modules held in RuleEngineImpl, L125’s concurrent map (L146). Event triggers are ordinary subscribers: GenericEventTriggerHandler, L49 implements EventSubscriber, and a match calls triggered(), L54, which submits to a per-rule sequential executor running re.runRule() (L86).
  • Discovery ends in an inbox, never straight in the registry. Bindings implement DiscoveryService.startScan(), L114; results fan out via thingDiscovered(), L359; the PersistentInbox, L96 stores proposals, and only the explicit approve(), L187 materializes a managed Thing.

Detail view: ThingRegistryImpl pushes tracker callbacks into ThingManagerImpl, which wires handler factories to per-device handlers; CommunicationManager resolves profiles per ItemChannelLink; the OSGi event bus connects items, rule triggers and the discovery inbox into one async fabric.

One bus, two object worlds

The design’s pivotal choice is that the “functional” world (Items, what users automate) and the “physical” world (Things, what bindings drive) never hold references to each other. ItemChannelLink, L29 is the entire bridge, and the ItemChannelLinkRegistry, L74 tracks it so relinking an item to a different channel is a registry mutation, not a code change. Consequences show up everywhere: renaming a device requires no UI edits, one item can draw state from several Things, and the same link table powers REST and UI alike.

The bus underneath is deliberately in-process. OSGiEventPublisher hands events to the OSGi EventAdmin running inside the JVM; there is no broker hop between a UI command and a device handler, which is why command latency is a thread schedule rather than a network round trip. If you need fan-out across machines you bring your own transport — the same trade-off we examined when comparing Redis pub/sub to local queues: in-process buses win on latency and lose on topology, and openHAB chose latency, then layered transports (MQTT, Modbus, serial) as separate bundles for the edges that genuinely speak protocols.

What a binding must actually provide

A binding author writes three things: a ThingHandler with handleCommand() and initialize(), a ThingHandlerFactory that claims its Thing types, and XML descriptions under OH-INF/ that the repo’s XML providers parse into ThingType/ChannelType objects — ThingType, L41 lists channel definitions, config parameters and supported bridges. BaseThingHandler, L69 supplies the conveniences (updateState(), updateStatus()) so driver code stays about the device, not the plumbing. Notably, this core repository contains zero device bindings — it ships the SPI, the transports and the marketplace installer machinery; the hundreds of protocol bindings are built elsewhere against these exact interfaces. That is how a bridge like Zigbee2MQTT can be consumed from openHAB without any core change: its MQTT topics are just another client of the MQTT transport bundle, one link table away from ordinary Items.

Rules are graphs, scripts are modules

The automation bundle models rules as connection graphs: trigger outputs feed condition and action inputs by name, with a separator constant (OUTPUT_SEPARATOR, L130) encoding moduleId.outputId references. The engine refuses to run a rule until every module type resolves and every handler attaches, exposing statuses like uninitialized and idle (documented on RuleEngineImpl, L107–113). Script actions (the model.script bundles) are just another module handler type plugged into the same graph — which is why a rule can mix a declarative trigger with a JavaScript action without the engine knowing either syntax. Disabled rules persist separately (DISABLED_RULE_STORAGE, L132) so a restart never resurrects something a user explicitly switched off.

From Eclipse SmartHome to 100 OSGi bundles

The lineage is written in the code. Comments still reference the Eclipse SmartHome tracker (NetUtil.java, L206), and several files carry “port to Eclipse SmartHome” author tags — the project was the Eclipse incubation that openHAB industrialized, and the package roots were renamed org.eclipse.smarthome → org.openhab.core along the way. The build mechanics reflect that OSGi heritage: the README describes the repo as “an artifact repository of OSGi bundles that can be used within smart home products” (L16) whose Maven build “produces OSGi bundles, dependency BOMs … and Karaf feature definitions” (L20). Concretely: 100 bundle modules under bundles/, each a bnd-built OSGi jar; the Karaf feature catalog at feature.xml, L20 assembles openhab-core-base, with transports like openhab-core-io-transport-mqtt, L280 and the rule DSL runtime openhab-core-model-rule, L346 as opt-in features. The version is 5.3.0-SNAPSHOT (pom.xml, L15) under EPL-2.0, and 27 itests/ modules boot real OSGi runtimes from itest.bndrun files (README L38) rather than mocking the registry — which is why service-wiring regressions get caught before release.

Standing next to its neighbors

Compared with Domoticz, which opts for a compact C++ core with Lua/Python scripting, openHAB trades binary weight for a formally versioned extension contract: bindings are OSGi bundles whose compatibility the framework checks, not plugins compiled against a moving header. Compared with Home Assistant, the difference is the same one the diagrams show — openHAB centralizes the event fabric in the runtime and keeps protocol handling in drivers, so the hub process itself stays protocol-agnostic. And for the radio layer, pairing this framework with a bridge such as Zigbee2MQTT keeps the two architectures cleanly separated: openHAB owns modeling and rules; the bridge owns mesh management.

Honest Limits

  • No device drivers ship here. The 100 bundles/ modules are framework, model and transport code; protocol integrations live in the separate add-ons repository, so this source tour explains the contract, not a specific device’s decoding.
  • The event bus is in-JVM only. OSGiEventManager subscribes to OSGi event.topics=openhab inside one process (L44); nothing under org.openhab.core.events serializes events off-box, and remote scenarios are left to separate bundles and deployments.
  • Discovery is binding-dependent. startScan() implementations live with each binding; core only defines the contract (L48) and the inbox, so scan coverage varies per protocol.
  • The rule DSL is part of this repo, but engines for scripts are layered. model.rule/model.script are Xtext language bundles in-tree; their runtime behavior depends on script engines registered as module handlers, which core does not provide.
  • All line numbers refer to main at HEAD 15c6da97b24e (2026-11-15) and will drift as files evolve; the architecture, not the line numbers, is the durable part.
entry.summary: How openHAB works: a source tour of openhab-core's OSGi bundles — Thing/Channel/Item model, binding SPI, EventAdmin event bus, rule engine and discovery.

entry.title: How Tasmota Works: Inside the ESP8266/ESP32 Firmware Architecture

link.title: How Tasmota Works: Inside the ESP8266/ESP32 Firmware Architecture

entry.content:
That smart plug still works, but the vendor’s cloud no longer does. When the startup behind a wall of Wi-Fi sockets shuts its servers down, the hardware turns into e-waste overnight: the relay toggle, the schedule, the energy meter all lived on somebody else’s VM. Tasmota is the escape hatch — open-source C++ firmware that replaces the vendor image on cheap ESP8266 and ESP32 hardware and drives everything through local MQTT. After the swap, relays, sensors, timers and automation all run inside your LAN, and the device answers to your broker instead of an app.

The two diagrams below map the arendst/Tasmota codebase on its development branch (version constant 0x10000004, i.e. 16.0.0.4, at the time of writing). The overview shows the layers: boot-time configuration, the cooperative scheduler, the xdrv driver framework, the command path, the MQTT telemetry engine, and the automation plus web layer. The detail diagram traces one command from an HTTP form field through the shared mailbox into the driver table and back out as MQTT JSON.

By the end you will know how 204 driver files coordinate without a plugin manager, why the whole firmware can reshape itself around a device template, and where the rule engine hooks into telemetry — every claim carries a line-numbered link into the repository, so you can verify each one against the tree.

Overview: Tasmota's firmware layers on the development branch — from boot flags to the driver table that MQTT, rules and the web UI all converge on.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • XdrvMailbox, L201 — the entire calling convention is one global struct: command, index, payload, data, topic, plus an MQTT5 context field. There is no per-driver callback API; interfaces fill the struct and drivers read it (instance closed at L214).
  • ExecuteCommand, L339 — MQTT payloads, HTTP form fields, serial input and rule actions all funnel into this one parser, which stamps the mailbox fields at L479 before routing.
  • DecodeCommand, L1173 — the core command table is searched first; anything unclaimed falls through to XdrvCall(FUNC_COMMAND), L491 and then to the sensor table, so driver commands and core commands live in one namespace.
  • xdrv_func_ptr[], L21 — the driver table is an array of up to 128 function pointers, and kXdrvList, L548 the matching ID list; both are assembled from #ifdef XDRV_NN guards, so the build itself is the plugin manager.
  • XdrvCall, L1156 — one call broadcasts a function code to every driver in slot order, but only function codes at or above FUNC_return_result = 200 (tasmota.h, L489) stop at the first truthy claimant (L1220); below that threshold the call is a broadcast, which is how FUNC_JSON_APPEND lets each sensor add fields to one JSON buffer.
  • Scheduler, L822 — the only loop that matters: loop(), L893 feeds it, it fires FUNC_LOOP at L823, then 50/100/250 ms and 1-second slices driven by TimeReached deadlines rather than sleeps.
  • PerformEverySecond, L1133 — the 1 Hz tick also probes driver liveness via XdrvCall(FUNC_ACTIVE) at L873; each driver’s verdict lands in the Xdrv_active bitmask (L1066), which is what the Drivers command reports.
  • MqttPublish, L1138 — every reply flows through cmnd/stat/tele prefix topics (L1167), and publishing runs the rule engine on the same payload via XdrvRulesProcess, L1246.
  • MqttPublishTeleState, L944 — telemetry is a counter, not a timer: when tele_period reaches Settings->tele_period (L1248) the accumulated sensor JSON goes out as one tele/STATE message, followed by FUNC_AFTER_TELEPERIOD housekeeping (L1254).

Detail: one command traced from the parser through the dispatch table into driver slots 01, 02, 10, 12 and 23, plus the telemetry counter and the rule re-entry path.

One mailbox, one table: the whole extension model

The design decision that holds Tasmota together is refusing per-driver interfaces. Instead, a driver is just a function bool XdrvNN(uint32_t function) with a switch over function codes, registered in the pointer table by adding one #ifdef block. The mailbox (struct XDRVMAILBOX, L201) carries the parameters of whichever interaction is in flight, and its fields are reused for everything: a command invocation, an MQTT payload, a rule event string. That reuse is visible in XdrvRulesProcess, L1087, which temporarily swaps XdrvMailbox.data for the event text, calls slot 10 directly through XdrvCallDriver(10, …), L1090, and restores the buffer afterwards.

The two thresholds matter. Function codes below FUNC_return_result = 200 are pure notifications — every enabled driver sees FUNC_LOOP, FUNC_EVERY_SECOND, FUNC_JSON_APPEND. Codes at 200 and above are claims: the first driver returning true wins, which is why exactly one driver answers FUNC_COMMAND or FUNC_SET_DEVICE_POWER. XdrvCallDriver, L1124 exists for the rare case where the caller wants to address one numbered slot directly, bypassing the walk.

The scheduler: one loop, four timers

There is no RTOS task per driver and no event thread pool. Scheduler() divides one cooperative loop into fixed slices: 50, 100 and 250 milliseconds plus one second, each guarded by a TimeReached deadline. The 1-second slice calls PerformEverySecond and immediately probes every driver with FUNC_ACTIVE. Sensor drivers therefore poll, they are never awaited — a driver that wants to behave asynchronously has to be written as a state machine stepping through these ticks, which is exactly how the Zigbee and camera drivers are structured.

The tail of loop() computes a rolling loop-load average and converts Settings->sleep into SleepDelay calls, so an idle device sleeps most of each second and still wakes in time for the next deadline — the dynamic-sleep behaviour behind SetOption60.

The MQTT telemetry engine

Driver slot 02 is the only component that speaks broker protocol, and it is deliberately thin: MqttInit, L268 connects and subscribes, and once the link is up it calls XdrvCall(FUNC_MQTT_INIT) at L1488 so other drivers can announce — that is the hook Home Assistant discovery uses in Xdrv12, L1252 to publish entity definitions. Inbound payloads on the command prefix are handed straight to ExecuteCommand; outbound answers go through the prefix-topic helpers, which is why the same RESULT JSON appears identically over MQTT, HTTP and serial.

Telemetry is aggregated centrally. Each sensor driver appends its fragment during FUNC_JSON_APPEND; the teleperiod counter then publishes the whole buffer at once, reducing flash-heap churn and broker traffic. Integrations hang off this same spine: the tree ships a dedicated Domoticz bridge driver (xdrv_07_domoticz.ino) for users pairing the device with Domoticz. Where ESPHome generates a bespoke firmware image from YAML, Tasmota keeps one binary and pushes behaviour changes at runtime — templates, rules and teleperiod are settings, not rebuilds.

The rule engine: automation inside the firmware

Rules live in slot 10 as a small interpreter over ON <trigger> DO <command> ENDON blocks. RulesProcessEvent, L880 matches the incoming event string against the stored rule sets; the Xdrv10, L2372 dispatcher receives it as FUNC_RULES_PROCESS (L2392). Crucially, the action part of a rule is not a special API call — it is re-issued through ExecuteCommand with source SRC_RULE (L839), so rules compose the same command surface a human uses from the console.
